'''''Cuscuta campestris''''', with the [[common name]]s '''field dodder''', '''golden dodder''', '''large-seeded alfalfa dodder''', '''yellow dodder''' and '''prairie dodder''', is a [[parasite|parasitic]] plant which belongs to the family [[Convolvulaceae]]. It was formerly classified in the family [[Cuscutaceae]].

It is native to central [[North America]]. It is a parasite of a wide range of herbaceous plants.

It is a pest of [[alfalfa|lucerne]] (alfalfa) and other [[legumes]]. It has become a widespread weed in many countries. It is known as 'golden dodder' in [[Australia]].

It has been confused in some recent literature with ''[[Cuscuta pentagona]]'' Engelmann, but the differences between the two species are clear.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Costea M. | year = 2006 | title = Taxonomy of the ''Cuscuta pentagona'' complex (Convolvulaceae) in North America | journal = Sida | volume = 22 | issue = 1| pages = 151–175 }}</ref>

The seeds of this plant have been found to become dispersed by waterfowl in significant numbers.<ref>{{citation |author=M. Costea |author2=S. Stefanović |author3=M. A. García|author4=S. De La Cruz |author5=M. L. Casazza |author6=A. J. Green |name-list-style=amp |year=2016 |title=Waterfowl endozoochory: An overlooked long-distance dispersal mode for ''Cuscuta'' (dodder) |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=103 |issue=5 |pages=837–844 |doi=10.3732/ajb.1500507|pmid=27208362 |url=https://digital.csic.es/bitstream/10261/133455/1/Cuscuta%20seed%20dispersal%20by%20waterfowlAJB_DigitalCSIC.pdf|doi-access=free |bibcode=2016AmJB..103..957C }}</ref>

== Description ==
The life cycle of the ''Cuscuta'' starts with seed germination. The seeds germinate near the surface of the soil, sending up thin pale green and yellow stems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cuscuta campestris {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://ipni.org/n/72786-2 |access-date=2024-12-09 |website=ipni.org}}</ref> The thread-like stems grow slowly until they touch another plant and begin to wrap themselves around it. Once fully wrapped around a host plant, ''Cuscuta campestris'' will form sucker-like roots, called haustoria, and penetrate the body of the host, stealing nutrients from them.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web |author-link=New Mexico State University |title=Dodder (Cuscuta spp.) Biology and Management |url=https://pubs.nmsu.edu/_a/A615/#:~:text=While%20small%20infestations%20can%20be,replant%20with%20non%2Dhost%20crops. |website=New Mexico State University}}</ref> If the seedlings do not make contact with a host plant, they will die.<ref name=":33">{{Cite web |title=Cuscuta campestris |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/cuscuta_campestris.htm#:~:text=western%20field%20dodder-,Origin,to%20parts%20of%20South%20America. |access-date=2024-10-23 |website=keyserver.lucidcentral.org}}</ref> The seedlings cannot survive for long  they find the appropriate plant stem by recognizing plant chemo-attractants. ''Cuscuta campestris'' is known for reducing the growth of their host plants.<ref name="ReferenceA">Ashton and Santana, 1976; Cooke and Black, 1987; Dawson et al., 1994 {{full citation needed|date=December 2016}}</ref> This mechanism gives them the ability to control other populations of plants such as ''Mikania micrantha''.<ref>{{citation |author1=Shen, H. |title=Influence of the obligate parasite ''Cuscuta campestris'' on growth and biomass allocation of its host ''Mikania micrantha'' |journal=Journal of Experimental Botany |volume=56 |issue=415 |pages=1277–1284 |year=2005 |url=http://jxb.oxfordjournals.org/content/56/415/1277.abstract |doi=10.1093/jxb/eri128 |pmid=15767325 |author2=Ye, W. |author3=Hong, L. |author4=Cao, H. |author5=Wang, Z. |doi-access=free}}{{dead link|date=May 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> Another mechanism by which dodders recognize which plants to parasitize depends on the light reflected off the host plant. ''Cuscuta campestris'' is highly attracted to "far red light", which is a wavelength that is reflected by most plant surfaces. Dodders that were exposed to unfiltered light were able to attach to their host before their energy had been totally exhausted, but dodders that were only exposed to red light lost their way. ''Cuscuta campestris'' is a parasitic weed that is one of the most widespread in the world.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Hong |first=Lan |date=2011 |title=The morphology and anatomy of the haustoria of the holoparasitic angiosperm Cuscuta campestris |url=https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1046/j.1469-8137.2004.00999.x |journal=Cabidigitallibrary|volume=162 |issue=1 |pages=147–155 |doi=10.1046/j.1469-8137.2004.00999.x }}</ref> It does not contain leaves or roots and must grow an absorptive organ as an interconnecting vessel between itself and the host plant.<ref name=":0" /> These absorptive organs allow for ''Cuscuta campestris'' to penetrate the tissue of the host plant and connect, drawing out nutrients from the host.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Koch |first1=Alexander M. |last2=Binder |first2=Christof |last3=Sanders |first3=Ian R. |date=April 2004 |title=Does the generalist parasitic plant Cuscuta campestris selectively forage in heterogeneous plant communities? |url=https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1046/j.1469-8137.2004.00999.x |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=162 |issue=1 |pages=147–155 |doi=10.1046/j.1469-8137.2004.00999.x |bibcode=2004NewPh.162..147K |issn=0028-646X}}</ref> ''Cuscuta'' spp''.'' can simultaneously parasitize different host plants, suggesting that the species may have a complex foraging strategy.<ref name=":1" />

Parasitic plants of the genus ''Cuscuta'' have little to no chlorophyll making them unable to significantly photosynthesize. This makes them photosynthetically inactive.<ref name="Johnson B. I. 2016 794–803">{{cite journal |author=Johnson B. I. |author2=De Moraes C. M. |author3=Mescher M. C. |year=2016 |title=Manipulation of light spectral quality disrupts host location and attachment by parasitic plants in the genus Cuscuta |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=53 |issue=3 |pages=794–803 |doi=10.1111/1365-2664.12627 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2016JApEc..53..794J }}</ref> ''Cuscuta'' species are thus referred to as holoparasitic plants, as they depend on their host plant for nutrients. About 10-15 species of ''Cuscuta'', out of the known 200, are considered agricultural weeds which wrap their vines around their hosts and obtain their nutrients from them through specialized organs called [[haustorium|haustoria]]. This mechanism for obtaining their food makes them very difficult to remove. Their growth has been cited to cause severe loss to crops that yield alfalfa, tomatoes, carrots and cranberry crops.{{citation needed|date=December 2016}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
The native range of this species is unclear but thought to be North America, specifically Canada, US, and Mexico. It is also found in parts of the Caribbean, including Cuba, Bahamas, Jamaica, Martinique, and possibly parts of South America.<ref name=":33"/> It is widely naturalised in parts of coastal and subcoastal regions of Australia, found predominantly in the Southeastern Australia along the Murray River.<ref name=":33"/> ''Cuscuta campestris'' can be found growing in grasslands, open woodlands, gardens, riparian zones, and wetlands.<ref name=":33"/> ''Cuscuta campestris'' has a tolerance for a wide range of climatic conditions, from warm temperate regions to subtropical or tropical regions.<ref name=":63">{{Cite report |title=Cuscuta campestris (field dodder) |last=Parker |first=C |date=2022-01-07 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.17111 |language=en|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Reproduction ==
Reproduction is through seed or vegetative spread. Pollination for ''C. campestris'' is autogamous, or self-fertilizing, and the species can produce up to 16,000 seeds on a single plant.<ref name=":63"/> In North America, flowering occurs in mid-summer, with less flowering occurring in humid, high rainfall locations. ''Cuscuta campestris'' seeds have a hard seed coating that requires scarification, reducing the danger of all seeds germinating at once.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cuscuta campestris (Field Dodder) - FSUS |url=https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/main.php?pg=show-taxon.php&plantname=cuscuta+campestris |access-date=2024-10-24 |website=fsus.ncbg.unc.edu}}</ref> Germination can occur regardless of the amount of light available, as long as temperatures are between 10-30 °C.<ref name=":63"/> The seeds are able to remain viable for up to 10 years in soil.<ref name=":63"/>

== Management ==
''Cuscuta campestris'' is an agricultural pest. By combining preventative, chemical, mechanical, and cultural methods, populations of ''Cuscuta campestris'' can be reduced.<ref name=":42"/> Scattered infestations can be dealt with using a hand-held flame gun, hand-pulling the host plants with the ''Cuscuta campestris'' parasite attached, or by mowing with a shallow blade.<ref name=":33"/> ''Cuscuta campestris'' must be controlled on vegetation located on roadsides and sidewalks.<ref name=":33" /> Because ''Cuscuta campestris'' is mainly spread by people, education to discourage carrying the plants to other locations is recommended.<ref name=":33" />

Preventive management includes planting dodder-free crop seeds, cleaning agricultural machinery before each use, and managing pre-existing populations to reduce seed dispersal.<ref name=":42" /> While small infestations can be removed by hand-pulling, the recommendation for controlling large infestations is to remove all plants of host species and replace them with non-host species.<ref name=":42" /> Field dodder can be controlled using pre-emergence herbicides, which are applied before ''C. campestris'' emergence, and post-emergence herbicides, which are applied after ''C. campestris'' emergence.<ref name=":42" /> Cultural control is another method for removing field dodder from an area, as planting non-host crops, such as wheat, broccoli, corn, sorghum, and legumes can significantly reduce its presence.<ref name=":42" /> Attempts to control ''C. campestris'' using biological controls include using gall-forming weevils (''Smicronyx spp.''), agromyzid flies (''Melanagromyza cuscutae''), or a pathogen, ''Alternaria cuscutacidae''.<ref name=":63"/> Once cleared, areas with a history of field dodder infestation should be watched for reinfestation.<ref name=":42" />

==Ecology==

''Cuscuta campestris'' is insect pollinated and is recorded to have been visited in northern Florida by ''[[Augochloropsis metallica]]'' and ''[[Augochloropsis sumptuosa]]''. <ref>Ulyshen, M. D., K. Robertson, S. Horn, and C. Dixon. 2024. Characterization of the bee community and pollination network in a southeastern U.S. pine savanna. Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 12:1403602.</ref>
